name: Git Basics
author: Recurse
subject: tools
description: Track changes with commits, branches, merges and remotes, and undo mistakes without losing work.

lesson.intro: Git records snapshots of your project so you can see what changed, work on ideas in parallel, collaborate without overwriting each other and get back to a version that worked. It is the first tool every developer uses on a team, and interviewers and new teammates assume you know it. This lesson builds a mental model of how Git stores history, then walks through the everyday commands and how to undo mistakes safely.
objectives: Move changes through the working tree, staging area and repository, and read git status
Create, switch and merge branches, and resolve a merge conflict
Sync with a remote using clone, fetch, pull and push, and fix a rejected push
Choose the safe undo for each mistake: restore, amend, reset or revert
Keep dependencies, build output and secrets out of the repository with .gitignore

sections.title: What version control solves
sections.body:
Picture a folder called `website_final_v2_REALLY_final`. Something you changed last Tuesday broke the menu, your teammate edited the same file on her laptop, and nobody is sure which copy is current. Version control exists to end exactly this mess.

A **version control system** records the history of a project as a series of snapshots. With it you can:

- go back to any earlier version, or see exactly what changed between two versions,
- see who changed each line, when, and the message they wrote explaining why,
- work on several ideas in parallel and combine them later,
- share work with a team without emailing zip files around.

**Git** is the version control system almost every software team uses. It is **distributed**: every clone holds the full history, so you can commit, browse history and create branches with no network at all, and every copy doubles as a backup. GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket host a shared copy and add code review on top, but Git itself is the program on your machine.

The unit of history is the **commit**: a snapshot of every tracked file at one moment, plus the author, a timestamp, a message and a pointer to the **parent** commit that came before it. Each commit is named by a hash such as `4e5f6a7`, computed from its contents. Change anything in an old commit and its hash changes, and so does the hash of every commit after it, which is why Git history cannot be altered quietly.

Read the diagram from left to right: each commit points back to its parent, and the chain of parents is the project's history. The labels `main` and `HEAD` are explained in the branches section; for now read them as "you are here".
sections.code:
a1b2c3d          4e5f6a7           8b9c0d1
(Add README) <-- (Add menu) <-- (Fix menu bug)
                                      ^
                                     main <-- HEAD
sections.tip: Set your identity once before your first commit: git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace" and git config --global user.email ada@example.com. Every commit records them.
sections.pitfall: Treating Git and GitHub as the same thing. Git tracks history on your computer; GitHub is one website that hosts Git repositories. Git works fine with no account anywhere.

check.question: Your Wi-Fi is down on a train. Which of these can you still do with Git?
choices: Nothing at all, because every Git command needs the server
Only read files, because commits wait for the network
Commit, browse the history and create branches
Commit, but only on the main branch
check.explanation: Git is distributed: your clone holds the full history, so committing, logging, diffing and branching are all local. Only push, pull, fetch and clone talk to another machine.

sections.title: Working tree, staging area, repository
sections.body:
You fixed a typo in `index.html`, added a new `about.html`, and also have a half-finished experiment in `style.css`. You want the first two in one commit and the experiment left out. Git makes that easy because every change passes through three places:

- The **working tree**: the real files in your project folder, which you edit as usual.
- The **staging area** (also called the **index**): the changes you have picked for the next commit. `git add` copies a file's current version here.
- The **repository**: the hidden `.git` folder, where commits are stored for good. `git commit` turns whatever is staged into a new commit.

You get a repository in one of two ways. `git init` turns the current folder into a new, empty repository by creating `.git`. `git clone <url>` copies an existing one, full history included.

`git status` is the command to run constantly. It names your branch and sorts files into three groups: staged ("Changes to be committed"), modified but not staged, and **untracked** (new files Git has never been told about). `git status --short` packs this into two columns: the left column is the staging area and the right column is the working tree. `M ` means staged, ` M` means modified but not staged, `MM` means you staged a version and then edited the file again, `A ` is a newly added file and `??` is untracked.

Staging captures a version, not a file name. If you edit `style.css` after `git add style.css`, the commit still contains the version you added; run `git add` again to include the newer edits.

`git commit -m "message"` records the staged snapshot. `git commit -am "message"` stages every change to files Git **already tracks** and commits in one step. It never picks up new files, so a brand new file always needs `git add` first.
sections.code:
$ git status --short
 M index.html
 M style.css
?? about.html
$ git add index.html about.html
$ git status --short
A  about.html
M  index.html
 M style.css
$ git commit -m "Fix typo and add about page"
[main 5c1e9a2] Fix typo and add about page
 2 files changed, 19 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)
 create mode 100644 about.html
sections.tip: git init names the first branch master or main, depending on your init.defaultBranch setting. Most teams now use main.
sections.pitfall: Forgetting that git add is a snapshot of that moment. If you edit after staging, only the staged version is committed unless you add the file again.

activity.title: Your first commits
activity.prompt: Run git status after every step and watch README.md move from untracked to staged to committed. Each commit adds a new dot to the graph, linked back to its parent.

check.question: You run `git add style.css`, edit style.css again, then run `git commit -m "Tweak colors"`. What goes into the commit?
choices: The newest version, because Git always commits the file on disk
Nothing, because the file changed after it was staged
Both versions, recorded as two separate commits
The version of style.css from when you ran git add
check.explanation: git add stores the file as it was at that moment. Later edits stay in the working tree (git status shows MM) until you add them again.

sections.title: Reading history and changes
sections.body:
A teammate asks: "When did the checkout page break, and what changed?" Git can answer that, if you know how to ask.

`git log` lists commits, newest first, with hash, author, date and message. The variations you will use most:

- `git log --oneline`: one line per commit, short hash and message.
- `git log --oneline --graph --all`: every branch, drawn as a graph. The clearest way to see where branches split and join.
- `git log -p cart.js`: the history of one file, with the change each commit made.
- `git show <hash>`: one commit's message and its full diff.

`git diff` compares two versions line by line: lines starting with `-` were removed and lines starting with `+` were added. Which two versions it compares depends on how you call it:

- `git diff`: working tree against the staging area, so it shows only changes you have **not** staged yet.
- `git diff --staged` (same as `--cached`): staging area against the last commit, so it shows exactly what the next commit will contain.
- `git diff main feature`: the difference between two branches, or any two commits.

Commits can also be named relative to where you are. `HEAD` is the commit you have checked out, `HEAD~1` is its parent, `HEAD~2` its grandparent, and so on.

Good history depends on good commits. Keep each commit to one logical change and write the message in the imperative, as if finishing the sentence "This commit will...": `Fix crash when cart is empty`, not `stuff` or `changes`. Small, well-named commits make the log readable, reviews faster and bugs much easier to trace.
sections.code:
$ git log --oneline --graph --all
* 9f3c2b1 (HEAD -> main) Fix crash when cart is empty
| * 7d41e0a (feature) Add discount codes
|/
* 2b8a6f4 Add checkout page
* 5c1e9a2 Fix typo and add about page

$ git diff
diff --git a/cart.js b/cart.js
index 3b18e51..a9c4f2d 100644
--- a/cart.js
+++ b/cart.js
@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
 function total(items) {
   if (!items) return 0
-  return items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price)
+  return items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0)
 }
sections.pitfall: Running git diff, seeing nothing, and concluding there are no changes. If everything is already staged, plain git diff is empty; check git diff --staged or git status.

check.question: Which command shows the commit two steps before the one you have checked out?
choices: git show HEAD-2
git log -2
git show HEAD~2
git show ~2HEAD
check.explanation: HEAD~2 means "the parent of the parent of HEAD". git log -2 lists the latest two commits, which includes the current one, not the one two steps back.

sections.title: Branches and HEAD
sections.body:
You are halfway through a new search feature when an urgent bug report arrives. Without branches, your half-done search code would ship along with the fix. With branches, the search work waits on its own line of history while you fix the bug on main, and you come back to it later.

A **branch** in Git is just a movable label that points to one commit. Creating one copies no files: Git writes a tiny file containing a commit hash, which is why branches are instant and cheap. When you commit on a branch, its label moves forward to the new commit automatically.

**HEAD** is Git's "you are here" marker. Normally it points to a branch, and that branch is the one your next commit will move.

- `git branch` lists branches and marks the current one with `*`.
- `git branch search` creates a branch at the current commit but leaves you where you are.
- `git switch search` moves HEAD to that branch and rewrites the working tree to match its latest commit.
- `git switch -c search` creates the branch and switches to it in one step. Older tutorials write `git checkout -b search`, which does the same.
- `git branch -d search` deletes a branch that has been merged. `-D` deletes it even if it has unmerged work, so use it with care.

Switching rewrites your files. If uncommitted edits would be overwritten, Git refuses to switch rather than lose them: commit first, or set the edits aside with `git stash` and bring them back later with `git stash pop`.

If you check out a commit directly, for example `git switch --detach 2b8a6f4` or `git checkout 2b8a6f4`, HEAD points at the commit instead of a branch. This is **detached HEAD**. Looking around is perfectly safe, but commits made there belong to no branch, and once you switch away they are easy to lose. Run `git switch -c <name>` first if you want to keep work you do there.
sections.code:
After git branch search (both labels on C, HEAD still on main):

  A <-- B <-- C  <-- main <-- HEAD
                 <-- search

After git switch search, an edit and a commit:

  A <-- B <-- C  <-- main
               \
                D  <-- search <-- HEAD
sections.pitfall: Running git branch fix, then committing, believing you are on the new branch. git branch only creates it; check the * in git branch or the first line of git status before you commit.

activity.title: Branch, commit, merge
activity.prompt: Before you switch back to main, predict what app.js will contain, then check it. When you merge, watch the graph closely: no new commit appears, main just slides forward to where feature is. That is a fast-forward, the topic of the next section.

check.question: What does Git actually create when you run `git branch experiment`?
choices: A full copy of the project files in a new folder
A new label pointing at the current commit
A new empty commit that starts the branch
A copy of the repository on the remote server
check.explanation: A branch is only a pointer to a commit, so creating one is instant. Nothing is copied and no commit is made; the label simply moves as you commit on it.

sections.title: Merging and conflicts
sections.body:
Your search feature is finished and tested on its branch. Now it has to join main. That is a **merge**: switch to the branch that should receive the work, then name the branch to bring in, as in `git switch main` followed by `git merge search`.

Git merges in one of two ways, depending on the shape of the history:

- **Fast-forward**: main has no new commits since search branched off, so main is simply behind. Git slides the main label forward to search's latest commit and creates no new commit.
- **Three-way merge**: both branches have new commits. Git compares each side with their common ancestor, combines the two sets of changes and records a new **merge commit** with two parents.

Git combines changes on its own most of the time, even inside the same file, as long as they touch different lines. It stops with a **merge conflict** only when both branches changed the same lines in different ways, or one side edited a file the other side deleted. It then writes both versions into the file between markers. The part between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` is your current branch; the part between `=======` and `>>>>>>> spanish` is the branch you are merging in.

Resolving a conflict is ordinary editing. Decide what the final text should be (yours, theirs or a mix), delete the three marker lines, save, then `git add` the file to mark it resolved and `git commit` to finish the merge. Until you add it, `git status` lists the file under "Unmerged paths" (`UU` in short format). If you get lost, `git merge --abort` puts everything back exactly as it was before the merge.

Conflicts are normal, not a sign that someone did something wrong. Keep them small by keeping branches short-lived and merging main into a long-running branch often, so the two sides never drift far apart.
sections.code:
$ git merge spanish
Auto-merging greeting.txt
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in greeting.txt
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

$ cat greeting.txt
<<<<<<< HEAD
Hello, world!
=======
Hola, mundo!
>>>>>>> spanish

# edit the file to the final text, remove the markers, then:
$ git add greeting.txt
$ git commit
sections.pitfall: Committing a file that still contains <<<<<<< or >>>>>>> lines. Git believes you when you git add it, so search for markers and run the tests before finishing the merge.

activity.title: Resolve a merge conflict
activity.prompt: Both branches changed the same line of greeting.txt. Run git status and read the markers before you resolve anything. After the final commit, look at the graph: the merge commit has two parents.

check.question: You are on main and run `git merge feature`. Both branches have new commits since feature was created, and they changed different files. What happens?
choices: Git fast-forwards main to the tip of feature
Git stops with a conflict in every changed file
Git refuses until you rebase feature onto main
Git creates a merge commit with two parents
check.explanation: Both sides have new work, so a fast-forward is impossible. The changes do not overlap, so Git combines them without a conflict and records a merge commit whose parents are the two branch tips.

sections.title: Remotes: clone, fetch, pull, push
sections.body:
So far everything has happened on your laptop. To work with a team you need a shared copy, usually hosted on GitHub or GitLab. A **remote** is a named link to another copy of the repository. When you `git clone` a URL, Git copies the full history, names that source `origin` and checks out its default branch.

Git also keeps **remote-tracking branches** such as `origin/main`: your local record of where `main` was on origin the last time you talked to it. They only move when you fetch, pull or push.

- `git fetch` downloads new commits and moves `origin/main` and the other remote-tracking branches. It never touches your own branches or files, so it is always safe.
- `git pull` is `git fetch` followed by merging (or, if you configure it, rebasing) the remote branch into your current branch. It changes your files. Newer versions of Git ask you to pick merge or rebase the first time the two sides have diverged.
- `git push` uploads your commits and moves the branch on the remote.

The first time you push a new branch, set its **upstream** so that plain `git push` and `git pull` know where to go: `git push -u origin search`. After that, `git status` also tells you how far ahead of or behind the remote you are.

A push is rejected when the remote branch has commits you do not have, because accepting it would throw those commits away. The fix is to `git pull`, resolve any conflicts, then push again. Do not reach for `git push --force` on a shared branch: it overwrites the remote with your version and deletes your teammates' work. If you truly must rewrite a branch only you use, `--force-with-lease` is the safer form, because it refuses when the remote has moved since you last fetched.

A typical day: pull main, `git switch -c` a branch for your task, commit in small steps, `git push -u origin <branch>`, then open a pull request so a teammate reviews the change before it is merged.
sections.code:
$ git clone https://github.com/ada/shop.git
$ cd shop
$ git switch -c fix-cart
# edit cart.js
$ git commit -am "Fix crash when cart is empty"
$ git push -u origin fix-cart

# later, back on main
$ git switch main
$ git fetch
$ git status
On branch main
Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 2 commits, and can be fast-forwarded.
  (use "git pull" to update your local branch)
sections.pitfall: Assuming git fetch updated your files. It only moves origin/... branches; your own main stays put until you merge or pull.

check.question: Which command downloads new commits from the remote without changing any of your local branches or files?
choices: git pull
git fetch
git push
git clone
check.explanation: git fetch only updates remote-tracking branches like origin/main. git pull goes further and merges into your current branch, which changes your files.

sections.title: Undoing things safely
sections.body:
Everyone makes mistakes in Git: a file staged by accident, a typo in a commit message, a change that broke the build. The right undo depends on two questions. Where is the mistake: in the working tree, the staging area or a commit? And has the commit been shared yet?

The table below covers the common cases. A few details matter:

- `git restore <file>` throws away uncommitted edits to that file for good. Git never stored them, so nothing can bring them back.
- `git restore --staged <file>` only unstages the file; your edits stay in the working tree.
- `git commit --amend` replaces the last commit with a corrected one: a new message, or a forgotten file you just staged. The replacement gets a new hash, so amend only commits you have not pushed.
- `git reset <commit>` moves the current branch back to an earlier commit. `--soft` keeps the undone changes staged, `--mixed` (the default) keeps them in the working tree but unstaged, and `--hard` deletes them along with any other uncommitted work.
- `git revert <hash>` creates a new commit that does the opposite of an old one. History only grows, so it is the right tool for anything already pushed: teammates simply pull the revert.

The rule of thumb: **reset and amend rewrite history, so use them only on commits that exist on your machine alone. Revert is for shared history.**

Your safety net is `git reflog`, a log of every commit HEAD has pointed to, including commits no branch points to any more. If a `git reset --hard` went too far, find the old hash in the reflog and `git reset --hard <hash>` back to it. Reflog entries stay around for weeks, but they are local and they only know about commits: they cannot rescue edits that were never committed.
sections.code:
Mistake                                Fix
-------------------------------------  ------------------------------------
Edited a file, want the last version   git restore app.js
Staged a file by accident              git restore --staged app.js
Typo in last commit (not pushed)       git commit --amend -m "Fix login bug"
Last commit was wrong (not pushed)     git reset --soft HEAD~1   (keep changes staged)
                                       git reset --hard HEAD~1   (throw them away)
Bad commit already pushed              git revert 4e5f6a7
Reset too far, commits missing         git reflog, then git reset --hard <hash>
sections.pitfall: Using git reset --hard to "clean up" while you have uncommitted work you care about. It deletes those edits permanently; run git stash first, or commit to a temporary branch.

check.question: Which of these loses work that even git reflog cannot bring back?
choices: git restore app.js when app.js has uncommitted edits
git reset --hard HEAD~1 right after committing everything
git commit --amend on your latest local commit
git switch main after committing on a feature branch
check.explanation: The reflog records commits. Uncommitted edits were never stored by Git, so restore discards them permanently. The reset and amend cases leave the old commit reachable through the reflog, and switching branches loses nothing.

sections.title: .gitignore: keep junk and secrets out
sections.body:
Run `git status` in a fresh JavaScript project and you may see thousands of untracked files under `node_modules/`, plus `dist/`, `.DS_Store`, editor settings and a `.env` file holding your database password. None of these belong in the repository. Dependencies and build output can be regenerated, OS and editor files are personal, and secrets must never be committed.

A **.gitignore** file lists patterns for files Git should not track. Put it at the root of the repository and commit it, so the whole team shares the same rules.

- `*.log` matches any file ending in `.log`, in every folder. A pattern with no slash matches at any depth.
- `/todo.txt` with a leading slash matches only at the top level, next to the `.gitignore`.
- `build/` with a trailing slash matches only directories named build (at any depth).
- `**/temp` matches temp in any directory, and `#` starts a comment.
- `!keep.log` re-includes a file that an earlier pattern ignored.

Ignore rules only affect untracked files. If a file is already committed, adding it to `.gitignore` changes nothing: Git keeps tracking it. Stop tracking it with `git rm --cached <file>`, which removes it from the repository but leaves it on your disk, then commit.

If a secret was ever committed and pushed, deleting it in a new commit is not enough, because it is still in the history for anyone who clones. Treat it as leaked and rotate the password or key right away. Ignoring `.env` from the very first commit is much easier; GitHub's gitignore templates for each language are a good starting point.
sections.code:
# dependencies and build output
node_modules/
dist/
*.log

# secrets and local settings
.env
.env.local

# OS and editor files
.DS_Store
.vscode/
sections.pitfall: Adding .env to .gitignore after it was already committed and assuming it is now private. It is still tracked and still in history: run git rm --cached .env, commit, and rotate the secret.

check.question: Your .gitignore contains the line `build/`. What does it ignore?
choices: A directory named build anywhere in the project
A file or folder named build, but only at the top level
Only a file named build, never a directory
Any path that contains the word build
check.explanation: The trailing slash restricts the pattern to directories, and because there is no other slash it matches at any depth. A leading slash, as in /build/, would anchor it to the top level.

keyTerms.definition: A project tracked by Git: your files plus the .git folder holding every commit and branch.
A snapshot of the tracked files with author, date, message and a link to its parent, named by a hash.
The actual files in your project folder, which you edit normally.
The set of changes chosen for the next commit, filled with git add.
A movable label pointing at a commit; it advances each time you commit on it.
The marker for what you have checked out, usually the current branch.
A merge where the receiving branch has no new commits, so its label just moves forward.
A stop during a merge because both sides changed the same lines differently; you resolve it by editing.
A named link to another copy of the repository; origin is the default name after git clone.
A local record such as origin/main of where a remote branch was at the last fetch.
A new commit that undoes an earlier one without rewriting history, safe for pushed work.
A committed file of patterns for untracked files Git should never add.

summary: A commit is a snapshot plus a parent link; the chain of parents is the history.
Changes flow from the working tree to the staging area (git add) to the repository (git commit).
A branch is a cheap movable label and HEAD marks where you are; git switch -c creates and moves in one step.
Merges fast-forward when only one side moved, and create a two-parent merge commit when both did; conflicts are resolved by editing, adding and committing.
fetch only downloads, pull also merges, push uploads; never force-push a shared branch.
Reset and amend rewrite history, so keep them for local commits; use revert for pushed ones, and git reflog to recover.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who saves files as report_final_v3.docx what a commit, a branch and a merge are in Git, and why git revert is safer than git reset for a commit the team has already pulled.

questions.question: Running `git status --short` prints `MM app.js`. What does that mean?
choices: app.js was modified on two different branches at once
app.js has a merge conflict that still needs fixing
A version is staged, and newer edits are not staged
app.js was moved to a new folder and then modified
questions.explanation: The left column describes the staging area and the right column the working tree. M in both means you staged a version and then edited the file again. A merge conflict shows as UU, not MM.

questions.question: Type the command that shows the changes you have already staged, that is, what the next commit will contain.
questions.explanation: Plain git diff compares the working tree with the staging area, so it shows only unstaged edits. git diff --staged (same as --cached) compares the staging area with the last commit.

questions.question: You edit the tracked file app.js and create a new file notes.md, then run `git commit -am "Update"`. What happens?
choices: app.js is committed; notes.md stays untracked
Both files are committed
Nothing is committed because notes.md is untracked
notes.md is committed; app.js stays modified
questions.explanation: The -a flag stages changes to files Git already tracks. It never adds new files, so notes.md stays untracked until you git add it.

questions.question: You have no uncommitted changes and run `git switch feature`. What happens to the files in your working tree?
choices: They stay exactly as they were on the previous branch
They change to match the latest commit on feature
They are emptied until you run git pull
Only files you staged earlier are updated
questions.explanation: Switching branches moves HEAD and rewrites the working tree to match the commit that branch points to. Switching back restores the other version.

questions.question: Type one command that creates a branch named `login` and switches to it.
questions.explanation: git switch -c creates the branch and moves onto it in one step. git branch login would only create it, leaving you on the old branch.

questions.question: The developer wanted this fix on a new branch, but it ended up on main. What went wrong?
questions.code:
git branch hotfix
# edit app.js
git commit -am "Fix crash"
git log --oneline -1    # the fix is on main
choices: git commit -am always commits to main
hotfix has to be pushed before anyone can commit to it
A branch cannot be created before the files are edited
git branch only creates hotfix; it never switched to it
questions.explanation: git branch hotfix creates the branch but leaves you on main, so the commit moved main. Use git switch -c hotfix, or git switch hotfix after creating it.

questions.question: You are on main, and main has no new commits since feature branched off it. What does `git merge feature` do?
choices: Creates a merge commit with two parents
Copies the feature commits onto main as new commits
Moves main forward to the latest commit on feature
Deletes the feature branch after merging it
questions.explanation: Because main has nothing new, Git can fast-forward: it just moves the main label to feature's latest commit. A merge commit is only needed when both branches have new commits.

questions.question: You fixed the conflict in notes.txt and removed the markers. Complete the step that tells Git the conflict is resolved.
questions.code:
git merge fix
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in notes.txt
# ... edit notes.txt and remove the markers ...
_____
git commit
choices: git resolve notes.txt
git add notes.txt
git restore notes.txt
git merge notes.txt
questions.explanation: Staging the file marks it resolved; git status changes it from UU to M. Then git commit creates the merge commit. There is no git resolve command, and restore would not mark anything resolved.

questions.question: A merge stops with a conflict in config.yml. Which situation caused it?
choices: Both branches edited config.yml, but in far-apart sections
Only the branch being merged in changed config.yml
Both branches made the identical change to config.yml
Both branches changed the same lines of config.yml
questions.explanation: Git merges changes automatically when they touch different parts of a file, when only one side changed it, or when both made the same change. It stops only when the two sides changed the same lines differently.

questions.question: A merge hit conflicts and you want to go back to exactly how things were before you started it. Type the command.
questions.explanation: git merge --abort stops the merge and restores the branch and files to their state before git merge ran.

questions.question: What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
choices: fetch only downloads; pull downloads and merges into your branch
fetch is for new clones; pull is for existing repositories
fetch uploads your commits; pull downloads other people's
There is none; pull is just another name for fetch
questions.explanation: fetch updates remote-tracking branches like origin/main and stops there. pull runs a fetch and then merges the remote branch into your current branch, which can change your files.

questions.question: Why was this push rejected?
questions.code:
git push
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'origin'
choices: You forgot to run git add before pushing
Your branch has no commits to push yet
The remote has commits you do not have; pull them, then push
Pushing to main is never allowed; push to a new branch
questions.explanation: Someone pushed to main after you last pulled. Git refuses because accepting your push would discard their commits. git pull brings them in; then your push works. Forcing the push would delete their work.

questions.question: Complete the command that pushes the new local branch feature to origin for the first time and sets it as the upstream, so a plain `git push` works later.
choices: -f
-u
--all
-d
questions.explanation: -u (short for --set-upstream) pushes and records origin/feature as the branch's upstream. -f force-overwrites the remote branch and -d deletes it.

questions.question: You ran `git add secrets.txt` by mistake. Type the command that unstages it and leaves the file itself unchanged.
questions.explanation: git restore --staged removes the file from the staging area and keeps your working copy. Plain git restore secrets.txt would do something different: overwrite the working copy.

questions.question: You run `git reset --soft HEAD~1`. Where are the changes from the commit you undid?
choices: In the working tree, but unstaged
Gone, deleted along with the commit
Moved to a new branch named HEAD~1
Still staged, ready to commit again
questions.explanation: --soft only moves the branch pointer back, so the undone changes stay staged. The default --mixed would leave them unstaged, and --hard would delete them.

questions.question: Complete the .gitignore line so every file ending in .log is ignored, in every folder of the project.
choices: *.log
/*.log
*.log/
logs/
questions.explanation: A pattern with no slash matches at any depth, so *.log ignores app.log and src/debug.log alike. A leading slash anchors it to the top folder only, and a trailing slash matches only directories.

questions.question: When would you undo a commit with `git revert` rather than `git reset`, and why?
questions.answer: Use revert when the commit is already pushed or shared. It adds a new commit that undoes the change, so nobody's history is rewritten. Reset moves the branch back and rewrites history, so it is only safe for commits that exist on your machine alone.
questions.explanation: Rewriting commits that others already have forces them to untangle diverged histories. A revert is an ordinary new commit, so everyone can simply pull it.

questions.question: What does a Git commit store?
choices: A list of the commands you typed since the previous commit
A snapshot of the tracked files plus author, date, message and parent
Only the changed lines, with no link to earlier commits
The changed files, kept only on the remote server
questions.explanation: A commit is a full snapshot of every tracked file (Git reuses unchanged files internally, so this is cheap) plus metadata and a pointer to its parent. The parent links turn commits into a history. Commits live in your local repository; no server is involved.

questions.question: Which of these problems does version control solve? Select all that apply.
choices: Getting back to the last version that worked
Seeing who changed a line, when, and why
Letting two people change the same project in parallel and combine the work
Finding and fixing bugs in your code automatically
Keeping passwords safe by encrypting the repository
questions.explanation: History, authorship and parallel work are exactly what Git provides. It does not find bugs for you (tests do that), and it does not encrypt anything: a committed password is readable by everyone with a clone.

questions.question: Put the states of a new file in the order it moves through them as you work.
items: Untracked: the file exists, but Git has never been told about it
Staged: git add put this version in the staging area
Committed: git commit saved the version in the repository
Modified: you edited it again after the last commit
questions.explanation: A new file starts untracked. git add stages it, git commit stores it, and any later edit makes it modified, ready to be staged again. The cycle of modify, add, commit then repeats.

questions.question: You are at the top folder of a repository. Type the command that stages every change in the project, new files included.
questions.explanation: git add . stages everything under the current folder, which from the top is the whole project. git add -A does the same from anywhere in the repository. Glance at git status first so nothing unexpected, like a .env file, slips in.

questions.question: Type the command that prints the history one line per commit, drawn as a graph, including every branch.
questions.explanation: --oneline shortens each commit to one line, --graph draws the branch lines and --all includes every branch, not just the one you are on. It is the quickest way to see where branches split and merged.

questions.question: You run `git add app.js`, then `git diff` prints nothing, although you definitely changed app.js. Why?
choices: git diff only compares commits, so you must commit first
git add saved the change as a commit, so nothing is left to compare
git diff needs a file name, as in git diff app.js, to print anything
Your changes are all staged, and plain git diff shows only unstaged ones
questions.explanation: Plain git diff compares the working tree with the staging area. Once everything is staged the two match, so the output is empty. git diff --staged shows the staged changes. git add never creates a commit.

questions.question: Match each command to what it shows.

pairs.right: Which files are untracked, modified or staged
Line-by-line changes you have not staged yet
Exactly what the next commit will contain
The commit history, one line per commit
The latest commit's message and full diff

questions.explanation: status is the overview, the two diffs differ by which pair of areas they compare, log lists the history and show opens a single commit.

questions.question: Why is creating a branch in Git almost instant, even in a huge project?
choices: Git copies only the files you changed since the last commit
Git compresses the project before copying it into the branch
A branch is just a label pointing at a commit, so nothing is copied
Branches are created on the server, so your machine does no work
questions.explanation: A branch is a tiny reference holding one commit hash. No files are duplicated, which is why Git users create branches for even small tasks.

questions.question: You run `git checkout 3f2e1d0` to look at an old version, make a commit there, then run `git switch main`. What happened to the commit you made?
choices: It still exists, but no branch points to it, so it is easy to lose
Git added it to main automatically when you switched back
Git deleted it the moment you switched away
Git saved it on a new branch named after the commit hash
questions.explanation: Checking out a commit directly gives you a detached HEAD. A commit made there belongs to no branch; Git warns you and prints its hash when you switch away. Rescue it with git branch rescue <hash> (or find the hash in git reflog) before it is cleaned up.

questions.question: You are on main and ran `git merge pricing`. Which value in this conflicted file came from main?
questions.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
const TAX_RATE = 0.08
=======
const TAX_RATE = 0.0825
>>>>>>> pricing
choices: 0.0825, the part between ======= and >>>>>>> pricing
0.08, the part between <<<<<<< HEAD and =======
Neither; Git shows the common ancestor's value first
Both lines came from pricing; main deleted the line
questions.explanation: HEAD is the branch you are on, so the top half (up to =======) is main's version and the bottom half is the incoming pricing branch. Your job is to replace all five lines with the correct final line.

questions.question: On main you run `git merge feature`. In which situation does Git create a merge commit with two parents?
choices: feature has new commits, and main has none since feature branched off
main has new commits, and feature has none since it branched off
Nobody has committed on either branch since feature was created
Both main and feature have new commits since feature branched off
questions.explanation: A merge commit is needed only when the histories have diverged. If only feature moved, Git fast-forwards. If only main moved, feature is already contained in main and Git says "Already up to date."

questions.question: Put the steps of contributing a fix to a team repository in order.
items: Edit the code, then git add and git commit
Open a pull request for review
questions.explanation: Get a copy, make a branch for the task, commit on it, publish the branch with an upstream, then ask for review. The pull request is where teammates comment before the branch is merged into main.

questions.question: You and a teammate both committed to main. Your push is rejected, and `git pull` then stops with a conflict in cart.js. What is the right next step?
choices: Run git push --force so your version of main wins
Fix the markers in cart.js, git add it, git commit, then push
Delete your local repository and clone it again
Run git fetch repeatedly until the conflict goes away
questions.explanation: A pull is a fetch plus a merge, so this is an ordinary merge conflict: resolve, add, commit, push. Force-pushing would erase your teammate's commit from the shared branch, and re-cloning would throw away your own work.

questions.question: You just committed with the message `Fix bugg` and have not pushed. What is the cleanest fix?
choices: git revert HEAD, then commit again with the right message
git reset --hard HEAD~1, then commit again
git commit --amend -m "Fix bug"
git restore --staged ., then commit again
questions.explanation: --amend replaces the last commit with one that has the new message. It rewrites that commit, which is fine because nobody else has it. reset --hard would delete the changes themselves, and a revert would leave two noisy commits.

questions.question: You ran `git reset --hard HEAD~2` and then realized you need those two commits. What should you do?
choices: Run git revert HEAD~2 to restore both commits
Nothing; --hard deletes commits permanently
Run git restore . to bring the files back
Find the old hash with git reflog, then git reset --hard to it
questions.explanation: reset only moved the branch label; the commits still exist. git reflog lists where HEAD has been, including the commit you were on before the reset, and resetting back to it restores the branch. restore only works with the staging area, and revert undoes commits rather than recovering them.

questions.question: You added .env to .gitignore, but Git still reports changes to it. What is wrong?
choices: The .env line needs a leading slash to take effect
.env was committed earlier, so Git keeps tracking it
.gitignore only takes effect after it is pushed
Files whose names start with a dot cannot be ignored
questions.explanation: .gitignore only stops untracked files from being added. A tracked file stays tracked until you run git rm --cached .env and commit. Because .env was in a commit, treat its secrets as leaked and rotate them.

questions.question: Which of these usually belong in a project's .gitignore? Select all that apply.
choices: node_modules/
.env
dist/
package.json
.gitignore
src/
questions.explanation: Installed dependencies, secrets and build output are ignored because they can be regenerated or must stay private. package.json lists the dependencies and must be committed, the .gitignore file itself is committed so the team shares it, and src/ is the code.
